title: Paging Dr. Sexiest Man Alive: Noah Wyle Takes PEOPLE's 2026 Crown After His 'Pitt' Comeback
excerpt: Noah Wyle is PEOPLE's 2026 Sexiest Man Alive: the 'ER' veteran turned 'The Pitt' Emmy winner takes the crown, succeeding Jonathan Bailey.
content:
Noah Wyle is PEOPLE's 2026 Sexiest Man Alive. The magazine revealed the choice on Amy Poehler's podcast Good Hang, with Poehler unveiling the cover shortly before Wyle joined her in the studio.

Wyle, 55, told PEOPLE he first thought the news was a joke. "I thought that sounded like a prank — just not in a million years did I think that this would be an honor bestowed on me," he said. He credited his wife, Sara Wyle, with convincing him to accept, saying she believes the kind of husband and father he is "is worth promoting."

The honor caps a remarkable second act. Wyle first became widely known as Dr. John Carter on NBC's ER, which premiered in 1994 and ran until 2009. He returned to the medical-drama genre as Dr. Michael "Robby" Robinavitch on HBO's The Pitt, a role that has earned him consecutive Emmy wins for outstanding lead actor in a drama series in 2025 and 2026. The series' third season is scheduled to premiere in January 2027.

Wyle succeeds Jonathan Bailey, the Wicked star who received the title in 2025. The annual distinction, first awarded in 1985, remains one of PEOPLE's best-known features. The announcement also links Wyle to his former ER co-star George Clooney, who has won the title twice. Wyle joked that Clooney would be "amused and feel, hopefully, like a proud papa, that I've come of gray-haired age."

Analysis: A Career Honor, Not Just a Cover

This title lands differently from a typical celebrity-crown moment because it reads as a verdict on longevity. Wyle spent fifteen years as television's earnest young doctor, then waited decades before finding a role that let audiences see him as a weathered, commanding lead. The Sexiest Man Alive cover is the pop-culture shorthand for that arc: the actor who once played the student is now the one running the room. It also shows how a prestige television performance can still break through the noise — The Pitt did not just revive Wyle's career, it reframed it.
